intro: Siliqua is a farming town in the south of Sardinia, in the plain below the castle of Acquafredda. In the countryside nearby grows an ancient olive that local people, a reader tells us, call the Queen: a trunk of twisted, hollowed wood wider than a car, which the reader puts at about a thousand years. Its age is the reader's estimate; we would love a measurement.
meta_description: An ancient olive near Siliqua in south Sardinia that local people call the Queen, about 1,000 years old by a reader's estimate.
question_meta: An ancient olive near Siliqua in south Sardinia that local people call the Queen, about 1,000 years old by a reader's estimate.
question_answer: The Queen Olive of Siliqua grows in the countryside near Siliqua, in South Sardinia, inside a low wooden fence. The reader photographed it from the ground beside its trunk.
question_context: Sardinia is olive country, and its oldest olives are among the oldest in the Mediterranean, their trunks twisted into shapes no young tree could make. Siliqua is a farming town in the south of the island, on the plain below the castle of Acquafredda, and in the countryside nearby grows the olive a reader sent us. Local people, they tell us, call it the Queen. The photograph shows a trunk that has become a sculpture: ribbed, knotted and hollowed, wider at the base than a car and wound round itself like rope, with silver-green branches still spreading overhead. That twisted, hollow shape is how an olive ages. Its heart rots away and the living wood grows on around the gap, so that a very old tree becomes a ring of columns twisting together. The reader puts it at about a thousand years and its girth at some ten metres, and adds a local story of Phoenician origin and a far greater age. All of that is theirs, not a measurement or a source we have seen, and olive ages are notoriously hard to pin down. The photograph shows a very old tree, worth the drive.

faq.a: An ancient olive near Siliqua in Sardinia whose trunk is a huge twisted mass of hollowed wood. A reader tells us local people call it the Queen.

trees.story:
"Local people called it 'The Queen'," wrote the reader who sent us this olive from the countryside near Siliqua, in the south of Sardinia.

The photograph shows why. The trunk is less a trunk than a sculpture, a vast twisted mass of wood, ribbed, knotted and hollowed, wider at the base than a car and wound round itself like rope. Olives this old split, rot from the inside and keep growing around the gaps, so that the living tree becomes a ring of separate columns twisting together, and this one has been doing it for a very long time. Silver-green branches still spread above it, and a wooden rail fence keeps the ground around it clear.

The reader gives it about 1,000 years and its girth at some ten metres. They add a story of their own: "Possible Phoenician origin, so graft considered the tree is 5,000 years old." Those are their figures and their story, not a measurement or a source we have seen; an olive's age is famously hard to settle.

If you know the Queen, her measurements or the name the village uses, tell us here.

Go in the morning, before the Sardinian sun is high, and walk slowly round the trunk.
